Putative hybrids from the natural zones of contact in Costa Rica and Guatemala involving S. humilis and S. macrophylla are intermediate in ecological tolerance and morphological characters such as rachis length and leaflet size. An extensive polyploid series of chromosome numbers is reported for the genus. Foliage Diseases

Cephaleuros virescens Kunze (Red rust): A parasitic alga reported on Swietenia mahagoni from India (Bengal) and Sudan (as C. mycoidea, presumably identical with C. virescens). Damage not known. A similar alga, C. mycoidea Karst., parasitizes many hosts and causes serious injury to tea and mango plants, particularly when it attacks young woody shoots.

Cercospora subsessilis Sydow (Leaf spot): Reported in India, Peru, and Puerto Rico on Swietenia mahagoni and S. macrophylla. Spots are 2-5 mm in diameter, zonate, tan, pale brown, or gray. No additional information available.

Colletotrichum gloeosporioides Penz. (Anthracnose): Associated with leaf spots and twig blights throughout the tropics on mahogany and numerous other species.

Meliola swietenia Cif. (Black mildew): Reported in the Dominican Republic on Swietenia mahagoni. Causes black patches on the upper surface of leaves.

Pestalotia swieteniae Gonz., Frag. & Cif. (Leaf spot): Reported in the Dominican Republic and the United States (Florida) on Swietenia mahagoni. Causes large, irregular, marginal or apical, reddish or gray lesions. Conidia are subfusoid, 22 x 5-7.5 microns, with 5-6 cells, and the middle ones have 3 setae up to 17 microns long.

Phyllachora balansae Speg. (Leaf spot): Reported in the Dominican Republic on Swietenia humilis.

Phyllachora swieteniae Petr. & Cif. (Tar spot): Reported in the Dominican Republic and the United States (Florida). Numerous black fruiting bodies in groups distort and disfigure the leaves.

Thread blight (cause unknown): Cobweb disease reported in Java on 22-year-old Swietenia mahagoni. Attacks branches on the underside. Affected parts are covered with a strong white mycelial cord, which occasionally divides to form a network increasing in density toward the top. The mycelial cord attacks petioles.

Text: A very large timber tree which has an extensive natural distribution in various forest types. This species is the most commercially important of the mahoganies. The level of exploitation has led to the exhaustion of supplies particularly in the northern parts of its range. The ecology of northern populations is relatively well understood whereas virtually nothing is known about Amazonian populations. Basic inventories are lacking for most of its range. Good stands apparently still remain in parts of Brazil and Bolivia. Regeneration of the species is stochastic, depending in nature on large-scale disturbance. This ecological strategy makes mahogany vulnerable to logging regimes. Harvesting and processing are generally only 50 percent efficient. There is, at present, little economic incentive to manage natural stands sustainably. International trade in timber of the species is subject to the provisions of Appendix III of *CITES.

BIOLOGY OF THE PHYLLOSTOMATIDAE

A 91-day period was observed, during which the temperature naturally cooled to 21°C at night. The relative humidity remained fairly constant at about 50 percent. At an elevation of 2,545 meters, where vampires do not normally occur in Mexico, Schmidt and Greenhall (1972:243) attempted to maintain laboratory conditions with temperatures between 25°C and 30°C and a relative humidity above 55 percent for Desmodus. Controlling an acceptable temperature and humidity at this elevation proved challenging due to power failures, which were worsened by the absence of a standby generator for emergencies. Typically, thermostatically controlled electric heaters and infrared heat lamps were used to maintain temperature, while cool mist electric humidifiers managed humidity. Uwe Schmidt (personal communication) reported that Desmodus thrived in his animal room in Germany, which was maintained at a constant temperature of 27°C and a relative humidity between 65 and 75 percent. Daily fluctuations in temperature and humidity can be monitored with a hygrothermograph, which should be calibrated with an accurate minimum-maximum thermometer, and a hydrograph, which should be calibrated with a wet and dry bulb hygrometer.

Ventilation – There is little information on the importance of ventilation and air circulation in laboratories housing bats. Pye (1967) cautions that many bat species are sensitive to drafts and over-ventilation should be avoided. In my experience, bats in poorly ventilated laboratories tend to appear restless.

Light – Light appears to be an important factor in regulating the daily activities of bats (DeCoursey and DeCoursey, 1964). Uwe Schmidt (personal communication) claimed that a colleague investigating daily bat activity found that Phyllostomus discolor, Carollia perspicillata, and Artibeus lituratus died when kept continuously in total darkness for 10 days. Illumination is often automatically controlled in many laboratories, and 13 hours of light followed by 11 hours of darkness has been found satisfactory for Phyllostomus discolor, Sturnira lilium, and Artibeus lituratus (Rasweiler and Ishiyama, 1973), Glossophaga soricina, Anoura caudifer, and Carollia perspicillata (Rasweiler and de Bonilla, 1972), Desmodus rotundus, and Diaemus youngii (Dickson and Green, 1970), as well as Desmodus rotundus (Schmidt and Greenhall, 1972). Many of the same phyllostomatids, except Diaemus, have been successfully displayed in a large simulated South American cave and tropical rainforest exhibit at the New York Zoological Park, where varying the intensities of white, blue, green, and occasionally red light reversed their activity patterns. Vampire bats maintained by Wimsatt and Guerriere (1961) were exposed to low-intensity illumination from light entering through two glass-brick windows and a glass panel in a door. The bat cage further reduced light exposure because only the front was made of transparent material. Electric lights in the bat room were turned on only briefly during cage cleaning or animal care. The researchers did not attempt to control the light regime, as wild vampires are found in roosts with varying light intensities.

More than 20 other reports have been published since 1974. Due to possible confusion with similar species, the Broad-winged Hawk remains on the ABC review list.

CRESTED CARACARA (Caracara plancus): Records outside known breeding areas include sightings at San Bernardino Ranch, COS, on November 10, 1979; Santa Maria Valley, YAV, on January 7, 1981; Sulphur Springs Valley near Elfrida, COS, on November 6, 1982; and in northeastern Phoenix, MAR, from December 6 to 23, 1991. These are just a few of the many extralimital records published since 1974. Sketch details are requested for inclusion in Field Notes.

BLACK RAIL (Laterallus jamaicencis): One male was found dead at Mittry Lake, YUM, on May 2, 1981. This species is locally common in summer along a short stretch of the Lower Colorado River Valley, with a few unsubstantiated sight records from southeastern Arizona. The Black Rail remains a review species for all reports outside the Lower Colorado River Valley.

PURPLE GALLINULE (Porphyrula martinica): Records include one at Willcox, COS, on August 7, 1975; one at Sabino Canyon, PIM, on September 11, 1976; one at Lehner Ranch near Palominas, COS, on June 1, 1981; one at Cook's Lake, PIN, from July 15 to 23, 1983; one at Gila Farms Pond, MAR, on August 1, 1991; and one at Picacho Reservoir, PIN, from August 8 to 14, 1993. Two additional records were published but not reviewed by the ABC.

AMERICAN GOLDEN-PLOVER (Pluvialis dominica): Records accepted by the ABC include single birds in southwest Phoenix, MAR, on October 24-25, 1974; August 27 to September 7, 1975; October 18 to November 15, 1975; and October 11-24, 1982. Other records include sightings at Parker, LAP, on May 6, 1978; southwest Phoenix, MAR; Willcox, COS, on May 23, 1983; Many Farms Lake, APA, on September 14, 1985; Tucson, PIM, on October 14, 1986; Ganado Lake, APA, on October 1, 1989; and Willcox, COS, from September 10 to 16, 1992. A specimen obtained at Kayenta, NAV, on May 10, 1984, is clearly identified as dominica. It is presumed that most Arizona reports are of this species rather than fulva, but past details and photos are often insufficient for definitive identification.

NORTHERN JACANA (Jacana spinosa): Two accepted records include one at Kino Springs and Guevavi Ranch, Nogales, SCR, from June 7, 1985, to January 3, 1986, and another at Mittry Lake, L.C.R.V., YUM, from June 6 to 30, 1986.

SOLITARY SANDPIPER (Tringa solitaria): One winter record was reviewed and accepted, of a bird in southwest Phoenix, MAR, on December 15, 1986.

WANDERING TATTLER (Heteroscelus incanus): The only accepted state record is of one in southwest Phoenix, MAR, from September 18 to October 9, 1971.

Cleaned_Text: In contrast to invertebrates, fish, and amphibians, nearly all bird species care for their young. Exceptions include brood parasites such as the brown-headed cowbird and European cuckoo, which lay their eggs in other species' nests so their young can be raised by the host species. Additionally, some megapodes, turkey-like birds such as the Australian mallee fowl, lay their eggs in large mounds of decaying vegetation that produce heat and incubate the eggs without further parental involvement. Text: The pathology hypothesis is generally refuted because it cannot explain why infanticide is observed regularly in some taxa even with low densities and little human disturbance (¢.g., primates; Hiraiwa-Hasegawa 1988). Rare occur rences of infanticide, however, might be caused by misdirected aggressive behavior in extreme circumstances (Hrdy 1979). The cannibalism hypothesis is not well supported outside of gulls and skuas because usually the victims are not eaten by the attacker (Mock 1984). Brood reduction often explains parental infanticide and has been reported in several bird species (€.g., Urrutia and Drummond 1990, Klosowski et al. 2002). Nonparental infanticide in birds often is explained by the sexual selection, resource competition, and parental investment hypotheses.

Text: En la Ckinantla se encuentran relictos de bosques mesójilos notables por su biodiversidad y endemismos; destaca la presencia de grandes extensiones de selva alta y selva mediana subperennifolia. media anual superior a 22 C), al semi-cálido (1 8-22 C), templado (12-18 C) y frío (5-1 2 C). Las lluvias, abundantes durante el verano, ocurren generalmente en las partes bajas de la región (20 a 300 msnm) y durante todo el año hacia las partes media y alta (400 hasta 3 000 msnm). En la Chinantla se encuentran relictos de bosques mesófilos notables por su biodiversidad y endemismos, y destaca la presencia de grandes extensiones de selva alta y selva mediana subperennifolia (Pennington y Sarukhán 2005). Parte importante de la cobertura forestal aún se encuentra en buen estado de conservación gracias al aislamiento relativo de los asentamientos humanos, pero también por el involucramiento y la participación directa de la población en el cuidado y aprovechamiento sustentable de sus recursos naturales. Sin embargo, los modelos de producción pecuaria y agrícola extensivos, así como el incremento demográfico, ponen en grave riesgo la permanencia de estas condiciones. Desde una perspectiva botánica, se estima para la Chinantla un total de 2 207 especies de plantas vasculares, lo que representa 26.3 del total de las especies conocidas para el estado de Oaxaca (García Mendoza ef al. 2004). No obstante, este número aún no se determina con exactitud y se siguen registrando nuevas especies para la zona, algunas de las cuales corresponden a especies endémicas, tales como el laurel Licaria chinanteca. Lo que sí se puede afirmar es que al menos 151 de las especies de plantas vasculares presentes son endémicas del estado, como algunas cicadas ( Dioon purpusii y Dioon spinulosum), orquídeas ( Prostechea vitellina ), bromelias ( Tillandsia imperialis) y heléchos ( Adiantum oaxacanum ) (Tejero-Diez y Mickel 2004). Otras especies vegetales no endémicas, pero representativas de la Chinantla, son el liquidámbar ( Liquidambar macrophylla), el ojoche ( Brosimum aliscastrum), el palo mulato ( Bursera simaruba), el cedro ( Cedrela odorata), el sombrerete ( Terminalia amazonia), el pino ( Pinus chiapensis), la caoba ( Swietenia macrophylla), el zapote mamey ( Pouteria sapota), la palma camedor ( Chamaedorea tepejilote), el barbasco ( Dioscorea composita) y el ixtle ( Aechmea magdalenae). Text: 256 Capital natural de México Vol. II: Estado de conservación y tendencias de cambio el punto de vista cualitativo (es decir, tipos o variedad de productos explotados), en todo el país se han identificado aproximadamente 5 000 taxa de plantas útiles y 215 especies de hongos (Torres-Rojo 2004), los cuales, aunque no sean elementos de la flora, se pueden considerar como recurso forestal no maderable. Solo en los bosques templados de Chihuahua, Durango, Jalisco, Michoacán, Guerrero y Oaxaca se ha documentado el aprovechamiento de 1 293 especies de plantas que pertenecen a 171 familias taxonómicas (Procymaf 2000). Desgraciadamente, buena parte del aprovechamiento de esta riqueza se hace de manera clandestina y muchas veces se restringe a una intensa explotación de unas pocas especies que ya muestran los efectos de esta práctica (Semarnat 2005), como se analiza a continuación. Desde el punto de vista cuantitativo, en general la magnitud de extracción de los productos forestales no maderables (pfnm) es considerable, y se estima que entre 1997 y 2004 se explotó un promedio anual de 60 000 toneladas de estos productos, con oscilaciones que van de 42 000 a 90 000 toneladas por año, lo que da un total de cerca de 558 000 toneladas (Fig. 5.2). De manera consistente, el producto con mayor representación son las resinas de pino de especies como Pinus oocarpa, P. leiophylla, P. lawsonii, P. teocote, P. herrerai, P. tenuifolia, P. montezumae, P. ponderosa, P. pringlei, P. michoacana, P. pseudostrobus y P. douglasiana, cuya distribución natural abarca principalmente los estados de Colima, Chihuahua, Durango, Guerrero, Jalisco, México, Michoacán y Oaxaca. Esta extracción representa de 25 a 50 por ciento del volumen anual, lo cual sugiere que estos pfnm se encuentran entre los más explotados. Muchos procedimientos de extracción de estos recursos implican la recolecta de individuos para su comercialización como unidades completas (por ejemplo, bromelias, palmas, yucas, orquídeas, cicadas, candelilla y cactos). En general, este tipo de explotación tiene como fuente principal poblaciones naturales que se extraen con escasos o improcedentes elementos de regulación. Por ejemplo, solo entre 2004 y 2006 se extrajeron 3 755 yucas o palmitos del desierto ( Yucca thomsoniana ) del Área de Protección de Flora y Fauna Cuatrociénegas (Profepa 2006a), una región donde la extracción ilegal debería estar controlada. Históricamente han existido pfnm que se extraen sobre todo en forma de partes de la planta (en contraposición con la extracción de plantas enteras), como consecuencia de su alta importancia económica. Tal es el caso de las palmas camedor o xate ( Chamaedorea spp.), las cuales hacia los años ochenta tenían un valor a precio de mercado en Estados Unidos superior a los 30 millones de dólares al año, lo que generó más de 10 000 empleos (González-Pacheco 1984). Solo el mercado norteamericano demandaba 363.2 millones de hojas de palma camedor anualmente. En la actualidad el comercio de estas plantas tiene un mercado bien establecido y constante (cec 2002). Sin embargo, y aunque se han desarrollado técnicas para su cultivo en viveros, la extracción ilegal es un problema persistente. Por ejemplo, en 2004 se aseguraron dos avionetas que transportaban de forma ilegal 55 512 hojas de palma xate, presumiblemente recolectadas en la Reserva de la Biosfera Montes Azules, Chiapas (Profepa 2004). Desafortunadamente esto no es exclusivo de dicha reserva en la Selva Lacandona. Por ejemplo, Ramírez (2001) señala que en Tamaulipas los bosques de la Reserva de la Biosfera El Cielo siguen siendo el origen de la mayor parte del follaje de Chamaedorea radicalis comercializado en ese estado. Lo mismo sucede en la región de la Chinantía, Oaxaca, donde alrededor de 50 comunidades extraen follaje y semillas, y 20 de ellas aprovechan alrededor de 1 000 toneladas de hojas por año (Ramírez 2001). Lamentablemente, dicho aprovechamiento se lleva a cabo de manera no sustentable y sin contar con un mercado que reditúe de manera justa y digna a los pobladores locales. Otro ejemplo ilustrativo es el de la pita (. Aechmea magdalenae ), una bromelia terrestre cuyo hábitat son las selvas altas perennifolias del sureste de México, que ha sido explotada históricamente por las comunidades indígenas y mestizas comerciantes del sureste del país para extraer su fibra a partir de plantas de las poblaciones silvestres (Edouard 2003, 2006). Las principales áreas de cosecha se ubican en las regiones de la Chinantla de Oaxaca, la Selva Lacandona de Chiapas y en diversas y pequeñas zonas del estado de Veracruz (por ejemplo, Los Tuxtlas). Aunque se trata de un recurso valioso, su rendimiento es intrínsecamente bajo, pues se calcula que para obtener 1 kg de pita se requiere cortar entre 250 y 350 hojas, y una hectárea de selva puede rendir de 15 a 25 kg de fibra por año (Edouard 2006). Esto hace evidente la necesidad de contar con programas de cultivo, extracción y comercialización sustentables que brinden beneficios netos y justos a los pobladores locales, dueños del recurso. Actualmente, aunque la demanda de pita se ha estabilizado, e incluso ha disminuido, en algunas regiones se empieza a vislumbrar el desarrollo de procesos de organización de la cadena productiva y de comercialización (Edouard 2006). La planta Euphorbia antissyphilitica, mejor conocida como candelilla es otro buen ejemplo del impacto negativo de la extracción sobre las poblaciones naturales.

En esta relación simbiótica, las hormigas ofrecen a la planta nutrientes y protección contra posibles herbívoros. Actualmente, se encuentran 21 especies de bromelias mexicanas en la Norma Oficial Mexicana (NOM-059-SEMARNAT-2001), diez de ellas endémicas para el país, tres en categoría de riesgo Pr (sujetas a protección especial) y el resto bajo la categoría de riesgo Amenazadas (A). Este proceso es el inicio de la cadena alimenticia del que dependen camarones, peces, cangrejos, crustáceos y ostras (Aniyar 2003). También actúan como sistemas naturales de control de inundaciones, barreras de huracanes e intrusión salina, así como control de erosión y protección de costas; además, mejoran la calidad del agua, ya que funcionan como filtro biológico al remover nutrientes y toxinas, contribuyen a prevenir la formación de suelos ácidos, generan condiciones de microclima, contribuyen a mantener sistemas y procesos naturales como respuesta a cambios en el nivel del mar, reservorios de carbono y mantienen los procesos de acreción, sedimentación y formación de turbas (Macnae 1974, Norudin 1987). Se calcula que por cada hectárea de manglar destruido se pierden alrededor de 800 kg de camarón y peces de importancia comercial al año (Turner 1977). A pesar de que la Reserva de la Biosfera Pantanos de Centla es una de las regiones más importantes por su ecosistema de manglar, la problemática continúa y se carece de datos precisos de su uso intensivo, necesarios para implementar estrategias de aprovechamiento sustentable. Recursos forestales no maderables West et al. (1985) comentan que, en el estado, en la época colonial se explotaban plantas como la pita ( Aechmea magdalenae), por su fibra útil para confeccionar prendas de vestir y cuerdas; la zarzaparrilla (Smilax sp.), importante por su raíz medicinal (como purgante y para enfermedades venéreas), y la pimienta tabasco, ( Pimenta dioica ) llamada allspice por su agradable sabor. Actualmente se desconoce el estado de las primeras especies; y en el caso de la pimienta existe el cultivo con problemas económicos sobre todo por el bajo precio de venta, pero no hay evidencia de sobreexplotación. Adicionalmente, una planta conocida como barbasco ( Dioscorea composita y D. bartletii ) fue muy explotada de los años treinta a los cincuenta por la utilidad de sus compuestos en el proceso de sintetizar anticonceptivos. Afortunadamente, se encontraron sustitutos de estas especies, por lo que dejaron de ser empleadas de forma masiva (Hinke 2008). Un grupo muy explotado son las palmas, ya que sus hojas sirven para construir techos habitacionales; otras por sus tallos tiernos, inflorescencias y por sus frutos. Ocasionalmente, el tallo se utiliza como seto y para construcción. De las 86 a 100 especies reportadas para México, 23 son útiles en Tabasco (Magaña 2007, Pérezeta .2007),cuatrodeestasbajoprotecciónespecial (Pr), siete amenazadas (A) y una en peligro de extinción (Chamaedorea tuerckheimii ; P). Es importante resaltar que la guayita de río ( Chamaedorea cataractarum) es endémica (semarnat 2010). En el listado de la nom059-ecol-2001 (semarnat 2002) se encontraban la chapaya y el tepejilote; actualmente cambió su estatus y quedaron fuera de la lista al comprobarse que sus poblaciones ya no están amenazadas (cuadro 2); sin embargo, se debe considerar que, al utilizar los tallos y los frutos, se disminuye la probabilidad de crecimiento y de propagación respectivamente, lo que ocasiona su disminución generalizada. Otro ejemplo de planta sobreexplotada es el motusay ( Philodendron radiatum), herbácea usada por los grupos étnicos chol y zoque del municipio Tacotalpa. De esta se aprovechan sus raíces adventicias para elaborar artesanías. Es una especie trepadora (hemiepífita) de la familia Araceae (Croat 1997); crece en forma natural en las selvas del estado sobre tallos, ramas de árboles, así como en pendientes rocosas y palmas (Bunting 1965). En los últimos años las poblaciones de esta especie han sido muy afectadas por diferentes actividades humanas, como la sobreexplotación y mal manejo en el proceso de extracción de sus raíces, así como la tala de árboles hospederos en superficies utilizadas para la agricultura y ganadería (Díaz-Jiménez 2006). En algu nas comunidades del municipio fueron implementados programas de desarrollo por diversas instituciones gubernamentales, privadas y de investigación, con la finalidad de apoyar a los productores y artesanos, iniciativas que resultaron insuficientes o que han dejado de operar. Desafortunadamente, no existen programas que apoyen la producción y el rescate de la especie; sin embargo, se considera que antes se debe tener un estudio acerca de su estatus, fenología y propagación para establecer un programa exitoso de rescate y apro vechamiento sustentable. In the Hall of North American Woods (Hall 26), ten new murals were added to those reported in 1939, increasing the total number to seventeen and completing the series that decorates three sides of the hall. These paintings depict human activities related to gathering, planting, and cultivating the most important types of vegetable food, as well as the preparation, transportation, and commerce of foodstuffs. Two of the new murals are maps. One shows the ancient trade routes over which products from the East were formerly brought to the Western World. The other illustrates the origin of the principal cultivated food plants in the Old and New Worlds. The entire series thus constitutes a pictorial story of food plants and enhances the interest of the botanical exhibits in this hall. 

These new murals, like those mentioned and illustrated in the previous year's Report of the Director, are the work of Julius Moessel, a Chicago artist well-known for his decorative paintings. Reproductions of the entire series have been published, with an accompanying text, in Botany Leaflet No. 25, The Story of Food Plants. An example is shown in Plate 16 of this report. 

The exhibits of North American trees and woods in C. F. Mills Paugh Hall (Hall 26) have been supplemented by the addition of many photographic transparencies showing forest types and land formations. Most of the photographs used were obtained by loan and represent a selection from the vast number of negatives in the files of the United States Forest Service. A few are from the Museum's own files, and others have been obtained from individuals and organizations such as the Redwood League, American Lumberman, etc. 

As in Hall 25, the presence of colored outdoor scenes greatly contributes to the appearance of the hall and to the interest of the related specimens. A few of the installations of conifers in the northwest quarter of the hall were recently rearranged to provide a more orderly sequence.

Bond of Chicago, and a fine specimen of West Coast mahogany (Swietenia humilis), a gift from Mr. L. Lind Petersen of Escuintla, Guatemala. From material received in 1937 from the Mexican government and other sources, the exhibit of woods from Mexico was increased by the addition of an assortment of eleven species, mostly from the Isthmus of Tehuantepec. Text: The Caribbean mahogany is found on the Caribbean islands and also in south Florida in dry or moist forest, often on limestone. Its natural distribution is hard to ascertain as it has been widely cultivated. It was the first mahogany to appear in the European market five centuries ago. Natural stands are extensively exhausted and the species exhibits high levels of genetic erosion.

Accepting Sir John Richardson's description, the skunk very closely resembles the wolverene. The body is stoutish, and stands low; the eyes being small, and the ears short and rounded. " A narrow white mesial line runs from the tip of the nose to the occiput, where it dilates into a -broad white mark. It is again narrowed, and continues so until it passes the shoulders, when it forks, the branches running along the sides, and becom ing much broader as they recede from each other. Text: Sexual-selection driven infanticide has been demonstrated in several species of birds. Both male and female House Sparrows (Passer domes ticus) have been observed committing infanticide to increase mating opportunities in a polygynous population (Veiga 1990a, 2004). Infanticide by females of two polyandrous species that demon strate behavioral sex role reversal (male care for eggs and young), Wattled Jacana (Jacana jacana) and Northern Jacana (Jacana spinosa), also supports the sexual selection hypothesis (Stephens 1982, Emlen et al. 1989). Stacey and Edwards (1983) also reported suspected infanticide by an immigrant female in a breeding group of Acorn Woodpeckers (Melanerpes formicivorus), which shared a communal nest; the immigrant female subsequently laid eggs in a different nest cavity. Female Tree Swallows (Tachycineta bicolor) also committed infanticide when replacing missing females at a nest (Chek and Robertson 1991). Infanticide was also observed by replacement male and female House Wrens (Troglodytes aedon) in Panama (Freed 1986).

Café claro; láminas liguladas, de 4.5 a 6.5 cm de ancho, agudas a redondeadas, serradas, densamente lepidotas. Escapo erecto, de 25 a 38 cm de largo, flocoso, con algunas partes glabrescentes, brácteas más largas que los entrenudos, enteras, negras y descomponiéndose inmediatamente después de la antesis. La inflorescencia es 1 (2)-compuesta, con un raquis de 12 a 20 (226) cm de largo, flocoso, brácteas primarias lineares a filiformes, todas, excepto las inferiores, mucho más largas, membranáceas y descomponiéndose; racimos con 2 a 5 flores estéticas, patentes, brácteas florales filiformes, de aproximadamente 3 mm de largo, más cortas que los pedicelos o casi del mismo tamaño que los sépalos, de 3.4 a 5 mm de largo, libres, asimétricos, esparcidamente pubescentes; pétalos azules a rosados. Esta especie ha sido registrada en Nicaragua por una sola colección (Grijalva 505) en bosques muy húmedos perennifolios, en la zona atlántica, a una altitud de 900 a 1000 m, en temporada de abril; también se encuentra en México y Costa Rica. Se distingue de A. mexicana por el tamaño de la planta y la longitud de los sépalos. Aunque estas características generalmente ayudan a diferenciar estas dos especies, los ejemplares robustos y los individuos delgados de A. lueddmanniana son difíciles de distinguir.

Aechmea magdalenae (André) André ex Baker, Bromeliaceae, 1889; también conocida como Chevaliera magdalenae André y A. magdalenae var. quadricolor M.B. Foster. Es una especie terrestre, que alcanza de 100 a 200 cm de altura en flor. Las hojas miden entre 200 y 300 cm de largo; las vainas son elípticas, escasamente más anchas que las láminas, enteras, de color café lepidoto; las láminas son liguladas a subliguladas, de 5 a 7.5 cm de ancho, atenuadas, serradas, glabras a inconspicuamente lepidotas. El escapo es erecto, de 48 a 84 cm de largo o más, blanco-flocoso, glabrescente, con brácteas divergentes a patentes o reflexas, más largas que los entrenudos, serradas, foliáceas. La inflorescencia, simple y digitada, está compuesta por 2 a 5 espigas de 4 a 15 cm de largo, con brácteas largas que superan los entrenudos, serradas, lepidoto-punteadas en la parte inferior, sésiles; los sépalos miden entre 35 y 38 mm de largo, son libres, en su mayoría asimétricos, atenuados, con lepidotos en la parte media y cínereos; los pétalos son amarillos, en bosques húmedos y muy húmedos, en zonas pantanosas de la zona atlántica, a altitudes de 0 a 500 m, en temporada de febrero a octubre, probablemente casi todo el año. Ejemplares recolectados en Costa Rica y México. Los indígenas extraen fibras de esta especie para fabricar cañas de pescar, sombreros, hamacas y sogas. Cuando está en estado estéril, esta especie se asemeja mucho a los miembros del género terrestre Bromelia.

Aechmea mariae-reginae H. Wendl., fue descrita en 1863. Es una epífita de 40 a 100 cm de alto en flor. Las hojas miden entre 70 y 90 cm de largo; las vainas son elípticas, hasta 23 cm de ancho, enteras en la proximidad, dentadas en la parte distal, densamente lepidotas café; las láminas son ampliamente triangulares a liguladas, de 8 a 15 cm de ancho, agudas a cortamente acuminadas, apiculadas, serradas, densamente lepidotas, con tricomas adaxiales frecuentemente coalescentes y exfoliantes. El escapo es erecto, de 10 a 73 cm de largo, glabro a farinoso-pubescente en algunas partes, con brácteas inferiores erectas y las superiores patentes, más largas que los entrenudos y que ocultan gran parte del escapo, serradas. La inflorescencia es simple, de 10 a 20 cm de largo, generalmente con 50 o más flores polísticas, flocoso-pubescente, con brácteas florales ausentes o angostamente triangulares, de hasta 4 mm de largo, más cortas que los entrenudos, flocosas, con flores sésiles; los sépalos miden entre 8 y 12 mm de largo, son fuertemente asimétricos, espiniforme-mucronados, con base flocosa, y los pétalos son azules en la parte distal y blancos en la proximal. Aún no ha sido colectada en Nicaragua, pero se espera que se encuentre en la zona atlántica de Costa Rica. Es la única especie dioica del género.

Aechmea mexicana Baker, descrita en 1879, también conocida como A. bernoulliana Wittm. Es una epífita de 60 a 130 cm de alto en flor. Las hojas miden entre 60 y 140 cm de largo; las vainas son ovadas a elípticas, de 8 a 14 cm de ancho, enteras o serradas en la parte distal, con una superficie que puede ser pajiza o café-rojiza; las láminas son liguladas, de 5.5 a 9 cm de ancho, con bordes serrados. El escapo es erecto, de 28 a 50 cm de largo, con brácteas erectas, aunque las superiores a menudo se descomponen después de la antesis. La inflorescencia puede ser 1 o 2-compuesta, con un raquis de 30 a 60 cm de largo, flocoso, con brácteas primarias enteras, las inferiores frecuentemente casi tan largas como las ramas de la inflorescencia o ligeramente más largas, y las superiores consistentemente más cortas, con ramas y racimos polísticos, patentes. El racimo tiene de 6 a 9 flores polísticas, patentes, con brácteas florales filiformes de 2 a 5 mm de largo, mucho más cortas que los pedicelos o a veces de la misma longitud, filiformes, glabrescentes, con pedicelos de 0.4 a 1.2 (hasta 1.6) cm de largo. Los sépalos miden entre 4.5 y 7 mm de largo.

Las capturas de túnidos fueron realizadas prácticamente en su totalidad por embarcaciones extranjeras, en proporciones que van de 91 a 99 según el año. Text: 512 La biodiversidad en Chiapas la diversidad de especies encontradas en el proceso de sucesión vegetal, la gran variedad de formas para su aprovechamiento y las posibilidades que se vislumbran para el desarrollo de tecnología silvicultural de las especies relevantes. El detallado cet maya-lacandón es capaz de reconocer la amplia distribución espacial de los árboles y las preferencias de algunas especies en relación con las condiciones que explora la agricultura, asimismo, este conocimiento resulta de gran utilidad para el desarrollo de estrategias de restauración al identificar las especies capaces de crecer en condiciones degradadas. Mario Adolfo Espejo-Serna, Ana Rosa López-Ferrari

Introducción  
La familia Bromeliaceae está constituida por cerca de 56 géneros y aproximadamente 3,086 especies (Luther, 2006), restringidos al Nuevo Mundo, con excepción de Pitcairnia feliciana (A. Chev.) Harms Mildbr., que habita en África. Desde el punto de vista económico, algunas especies como la piña (Ananas sativa Schult. f.), el timbiriche (Bromelia karatas L.), la pita (Aechmea magdalenae André ex Baker) o el heno (Tillandsia usneoides L.) son importantes, ya que generan recursos a nivel local y representan una fuente de ingresos alternativa para muchas comunidades. Además, en el caso de la piña, forma una parte fundamental de la economía estatal.  

En cuanto a su clasificación, la familia se ha dividido tradicionalmente en tres subfamilias: Pitcairnioideae, Bromelioideae y Tillandsioideae, las cuales están representadas en Veracruz. La monofilia de la familia ha sido corroborada por distintos estudios tanto morfológicos (Dahlgren et al., 1985) como moleculares con ADN de cloroplasto (cpDNA), aunque los grupos recuperados presentan diferentes composiciones en las subfamilias (Ranker et al., 1990; Chase et al., 1993, 1995a; Barfuss et al., 2005).  

Diversidad  
De los géneros presentes en México, Ursulaea, con dos especies, es endémico. Hechtia tiene su centro de diversidad en el país, con 50 de las 53 especies.

La pita se cultiva en comunidades de Oaxaca, Chiapas y Veracruz. Con el incremento de la demanda de la artesanía piteada a principios de los 90, cada vez más comunidades han establecido plantaciones de pita. In the coconut groves and around mango trees, the homes of Finsch Parrots (Amazona finschi), White-fronted Parrots (Amazona albifrons), Red- and Blue-headed Parakeets (Cyanoliseus canicularis), and the Military Macaw (Ara militaris) could be found.

When I first saw this bird, it was perched on a bamboo twig and seemed to be completely exhausted. We tried to save the bird. However, on that rain-soaked, breezy, cloudy evening an evening difficult for local migratory birds the kingfisher was soon found to be dead. Mr. Ramesh Salunke, a taxidermist of the Zoological Survey of India, while skinning the bird, noticed fine fissures and cracks on the skull. From these head injuries it appeared that the bird had hit against something. Dr. Savita Paknikar, a pathologist, found nothing in the stomach that could have contributed to its death. During the monsoons, the threetoed kingfisher is occasionally seen in the dry deciduous forests of the Sinhagad valley about 20 km southwest of Pune. The female had now come out of the nest and on March 20, 1 997, 1 saw a hoopoe, probably a male, constantly pecking at the entrance of the nest. 1 saw it trying to go inside the nest in which it finally succeeded. I was deeply overwhelmed upon seeing this bird, which usually inhabits moist deciduous and evergreen forests and resides close to water bodies like streams and rivulets. During the monsoon, this bird disperses widely and often dies by dashing against walls or window shutters. When I first saw the bird, it was perched on a bamboo twig and appeared to be completely exhausted. We tried to save it; however, on that rain-soaked, breezy, cloudy evening—an especially difficult time for local migratory birds—the kingfisher was soon found to be dead. Mr. Ramesh Salunke, a taxidermist at the Zoological Survey of India, noticed fine fissures and cracks on the skull while skinning the bird. These head injuries suggested that the bird had hit against something. Dr. Savita Paknikar, a pathologist, found nothing in the stomach that could have contributed to its death. During the monsoons, the threetoed kingfisher is occasionally seen in the dry deciduous forests of the Sinhagad Valley, about 20 km southwest of Pune.

**11. Infanticide in Hoopoe (Upupa epops Linnaeus)**  
During a stay at Corbett Tiger Reserve in Uttar Pradesh, India, I observed interesting behavior in hoopoes. I stayed at Dhikala in a house with a wooden floor that had numerous crevices. According to the residents, a pair of hoopoes would nest in one of these holes almost every year. On March 3, 1997, the first nesting was observed. After a few days, the female began incubating while the male brought her food. Sometimes, the male would bring food—usually grubs, termites, etc.—almost forty times a day. After about two weeks, the chicks hatched, and faint noises could be heard from inside the hole. The female had now left the nest, and on March 20, 1997, I saw a hoopoe, probably a male, repeatedly pecking at the entrance of the nest. It eventually succeeded in entering the nest, seemingly pecking at something, as drumming noises could be heard. After some time, it came out with some feathers in its beak, which it promptly threw down. It then went back inside and emerged with a live chick, which was also thrown down. The robbing continued, and the male managed to come out with an egg, which was also discarded. Such systematic killing of dependent offspring by replacing males is widespread among animals and has been reported in several primate species, such as langurs (Presbytis entellus), lions (Panthera leo), as well as in captive rodents like collared lemmings (Dicrostonyx groenlandicus), and among birds such as barn swallows (Hirundo rustica), house wrens (Troglodytes aedon), house sparrows (Passer domesticus), and female Northern jacanas (Jacana spinosa), as reported by Rowher (1986).

The Mexican Jacana (Jacana spinosa) is a very peculiar species measuring about 8 inches. It has a plover-like bill with a leaf-like sheaf at the base that covers the forehead. There is a hard spur on the shoulder of each wing. Its legs and toes are extremely long, with the toenails being abnormally large; the hind nail often measures an inch and a half. Young birds are very different from adults. They are grayish-brown above, with wings that are greenish-yellow, similar to adults. Below, they are whitish, darker across the breast and on the sides, with a light line above the eye.

Jacanas inhabit marshy, muddy pools and ponds, where they can easily run over the surface due to their long toes, which provide good footing on floating aquatic plants. They are known to be very pugnacious in defense of their young and are also known to fight among themselves during the mating season.

Nests are made of weeds and trash, built on little floating islands or lily pads. They lay 3 to 5 olive-colored eggs, which are curiously scrawled with black. The eggs measure approximately 1.20 by 0.95 inches. The Mexican Jacana is found and breeds within our borders only in southern Texas.

**Larger Mammals Around Kajiado**

**Large Herbivores**

Kajiado is at the south end of the Athi-Kaputiei plains, which used to be famous for their abundant wildlife. In the ten years since I first went to live in Kajiado, the numbers of animals have noticeably declined. The Veterinary Officer who was in Kajiado when I first arrived, Dr. Rudi Eugster, told me that in the six years he had been there, the "plains game" had greatly decreased. Thus, the decline apparently dates back to 1970 or earlier.

The most common antelopes are Thomson's and Grant's gazelles, with impala and eland in better wooded areas. Large herds of zebra, wildebeest, and hartebeest used to be common, especially after the rains, and were quite a hazard when driving at night. Giraffes are usually discreetly hidden in riverine bush but sometimes come out onto the plains to browse on the tops of the rather stunted bushes of Acacia drepanolobium. Dik-dik are still abundant in the riverine bush, as evidenced by their numerous latrines of tiny pellets resembling heaps of seeds. These animals can be seen in the early morning and late evening but seem to be invisible at other times. Warthogs are also present but very shy. On the hills south and east of Kajiado, mountain reedbuck are quite common, and klipspringers can occasionally be seen. Hyrax are also locally abundant in rocky sites.

This includes our Bob-white and the Masked Bob-white of northern Sonora, and formerly, at least, southern Arizona, the Scaled, Mearns and Gambel s Quails of our Mexican border States, and the California Valley and Mountain uails. . In eastern North America we have only one species, our familiar Bob-white, not, as we are apt to imagine it, a distinctively North American bird, but the most northern representative of a type whose stronghold is in Mexico where ten forms of the genus Colinus are known.

American Quail (Fig. 44): The members of this family, numbering about sixty species, are the American representatives of the Old World Perdicide, or true Quails and Partridges. Structurally, they are closely related, though they differ in external appearance. It is believed that both families originated from a common ancestor, similar to how Old and New World pigeons, parrots, or spoonbills are related. During the later Tertiary Period, when the climate was warmer in Arctic regions, their ranges were likely continuous.

Text: The Mexican jacana was described originally from Cartagena, Colombia, and as that remains still the only record for the country, the ascription to this locality was probably an error. The species is known from Divala, Panama (Bangs), and thence north on the Pacific side to Mazatlan, Mexico (Lawrence), and on the Gulf side to the mouth of the Rio Grande (Merrill). It is recorded from Porto Rico (Gundlach), Haiti (Ritter), Jamaica (Denny), and Cuba (Vigors)-rare in the first three and common in Cuba. Jacanas: Jacanidae

Jacana spinosa of A.O.U. check-list, 1957 (see Appendix A). A rather small, delicate marsh bird with a moderately long, rail-like bill; long greenish legs with extremely long toes and toenails. In flight or with wings lifted, the greenish-yellow primaries and secondaries are especially conspicuous. 

Adult: yellow bill, frontal shield (three-lobed in the Central American race), and wingspan; dark maroon above and below with a black head, neck, and breast. 

Immature: orange-brown bill; rudimentary frontal shield and wing-spur; grayish-brown above with a black nape and streaks behind the eye; white below, narrowly black on the sides. 

Length: approximately 9.42 inches; wingspan: about 12 inches.

Range: Irregularly from the coastal plain of Texas, chiefly in lowland tropics from southern Sinaloa and Tamaulipas through Mexico and Central America to Colombia, Ecuador, northern Argentina, and Uruguay; also in the Greater Antilles.

TEXAS: Breeding has been recorded in five localities: Cameron County, near Olmito (young, October 2, 1938); Cameron County, 6 miles south of San Benito (three downy young, August 24, 1951); Kleberg County, a small marsh just west of Cayo del Grullo about 4 miles north of Vattmannville (a chick, August 1–September 5, 1968); Bexar County, Mitchell Lake (nest with three eggs, June 25, 1922); Brazoria County, Maner Lake Club, 9 miles northwest of Angleton (three immatures said to have hatched on the lake in summer 1971, and three young observed in July 1972). Birds have apparently been resident on the lake since at least 1967; in that year, one adult and one young were shot—one was eaten, and the other preserved in a freezer for two years until properly identified.

Dispersal: Rare visitor in the Rio Grande delta; casual elsewhere in South Texas brush country, north to Uvalde (U.S. Fish Hatchery), San Antonio, and Victoria, and along the coast to Brazoria National Wildlife Refuge. 

Winter: Rare, at least formerly, in the Rio Grande delta; the Maner Lake population (at least six individuals) appears to be resident, observed during the winter of 1971–72.

Habits and Habitats: The slender, thin-necked Jacana inhabits marshes, where its grotesquely long toes and toenails enable it to walk agilely on floating vegetation such as lily, lotus, waterlettuce, and waterhyacinth that grow profusely in quiet freshwater of tropical lowlands. This curious walking behavior has earned colloquial names like lily trotters and lotus birds for the Jacanidae, a pantropical family of seven species. 

The Jacana places its nest raft among pond and resaca plants, but it is exceedingly rare for a Texan to witness the female incubating the elaborately marked eggs or tending the artistically decorated chicks. Like many other long-legged water birds—such as herons, egrets, storks, ibises, and spoonbills—most postnuptial northward migrants are in immature plumage; thus, about 75 percent of the few Jacanas seen in Texas are young. 

The bird usually appears singly but near other freshwater marsh inhabitants—especially Least Grebes, Purple and Common gallinules, and American Coots. Its raillike flight with dangling feet is seldom sustained; movement is generally limited to short gliding launches, usually low to the ground or water. When on shore, wading, or striding on floating plants, it forages for food.

Text: RUDDY TURNSTONE (Arenaria interpres morinella). Turnstones are unusual in form, in that the bill is quite stout, pointed and has an upturned appearance since the top of the upper mandible is perfectly straight. The present handsome species breeds on the Arctic coast and migrates abundantly along both coasts, wintering from southern United States southward. The common Turnstone, a grayer variety, is an Old World species, a few of which breed in western Alaska and migrate through Japan. The Turnstone is commonly known among sportsmen as Calico-back, Horse-foot Snipe and Beach Snipe.

Dr. J. Anderson on Spalax typhlus

On June 14, Mr. Sclater also visited the private menagerie of the Society’s Corresponding Member, Mr. F. E. Blaauw, of Westerveld, Graveland, Hilversum. There, he admired a beautiful herd of White-tailed Gnus, flocks of Rheas of both species (Rhea americana and R. darwini), and a fine series of waterfowl. A pair of Mantchurian Cranes (Grus viridirostris) were observed engaged in incubation, along with Bernicla poliocephala and B. rubidiceps with recently hatched young.

A communication was read from Mr. T. D. A. Cockerell, F.Z.S., of the Institute of Jamaica, describing the occurrence of a Jacana (Jacana spinosa, Cory, B. W. I. p252) in Jamaica. On April 20, 1892, Dr. Alex. G. McCatty of Montego Bay, Jamaica, sent a specimen of this bird to Mr. F. Cundall, Secretary of the Jamaica Institute, noting that it was entirely new to him and had been shot by his friend Mr. Dillon at Savanna-la-Mar, where it is known locally as the Banana or Plantain Coot. This was, as far as Mr. Cockerell knew, the first confirmed record of the Jacana in Jamaica.

However, in the Museum of the Institute of Jamaica, there is a skin of a Jacana presented by Mr. H. O. Vickers in 1886, which was said to have been shot by him in Westmoreland Parish, Jamaica. In a subsequent letter dated May 14, Mr. Cockerell wrote that, since his initial report, he had learned from Mr. R. A. Walcott, Resident Magistrate for Westmoreland, that the Jacana is definitely resident in Jamaica. It was first observed by a group of gentlemen, including Mr. Walcott, in 1874 on the Cabaritta River. Since then, it has been seen regularly in the Meylersfield Morasses, between Savanna-la-Mar and Little London, along the banks of the Cabaritta, and at ponds near Black River in St. Elizabeth.

Although there is no record of its importation, it seems likely that the species was introduced to Jamaica from the mainland around 1873, as the numerous sportsmen of Westmoreland and St. Elizabeth would have surely noticed it if it had been present earlier. Its arrival by natural means appears unlikely, since Mr. Walcott reports that it cannot fly long distances.

Dr. J. Anderson, F.R.S., F.Z.S., also shared notes on the occurrence of Spalax typhlus in Africa. Towards the end of April, while in Lower Egypt, he found a rodent in the district of Mariut, west of the Great Lake of the same name and about eight miles from Alexandria.

Text: NOTES A NORTHERN JACANA IN TRANS-PECOS TEXAS SARTOR O. WILLIAMS III, Route 10, Box 476, Glenwood, New Mexico 88039 At 0945 on 7 October 1982, Melissa J. Renfro and I found a single Northern Jacana ( Jacana spinosa) on a pond at a site known as The Post (elev. 1200 m), located at the end of a county road about 8 km south-southwest of Marathon, Brewster County, Texas. We watched the bird, which was in typical immature plummage, for about 45 minutes, then we left the area. We returned that afternoon (1430-1900) and obtained a series of 27 color slides of the bird; representative slides were subsequently verified and deposited in the Texas Photo-Record File as No. 404, a-d (Texas Cooperative Wildlife Collections, Texas A M University, College Station, TX 77843). The jacana was still present at the site on 11 October 1982, when it was seen by Geth and Edmund White of Alpine, Texas. 1 do not know if the bird was seen after that date; it was not present when I next visited the site on 18 October 1982. The small (90 m x 13 m) pond was the result of a low dam across Pena Creek and seemed to be several decades old. Cattails ( Typha ) bordered the open water, which was almost completely choked with a dense stand of pondweed ( Potomogeton ) , the pondweed forming a solid mat just below the surface. The jacana spent most of its time walking about on the vegetation mat and feeding actively, presumably on aquatic insects. At one point, however, it captured, dispatched, and consumed a large dragonfly. The bird was wary and alert and would fly to the center of the pond, calling loudly, if approached too closely or otherwise disturbed. There it would remain, watchful for a while, before resuming its feeding. Marathon lies about equidistant (some 800 km) from resident Northern Jacana populations on the west coast in Sinoloa and on the east coast in southern Texas and Tamaulipas; it is less than half again as far from resident populations on the Mexican Plateau due south in Guanajuato. NOTES ON A NORTHERN JACANA IN TRANS-PECOS TEXAS

O. WILLIAMS III, Route 10, Box 476, Glenwood, New Mexico 88039

At 0945 on October 7, 1982, Melissa J. Renfro and I found a single Northern Jacana (Jacana spinosa) on a pond at a site known as The Post (elevation 1200 m), located at the end of a county road about 8 km south-southwest of Marathon, Brewster County, Texas. We observed the bird, which was in typical immature plumage, for about 45 minutes before leaving the area. We returned that afternoon (1430–1900) and obtained a series of 27 color slides of the bird; representative slides were subsequently verified and deposited in the Texas Photo-Record File as No. 404, a–d (Texas Cooperative Wildlife Collections, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX 77843). The jacana was still present at the site on October 11, 1982, when it was seen by Geth and Edmund White of Alpine, Texas. I do not know if the bird was seen after that date; it was not present during my next visit on October 18, 1982.

The small pond (90 m x 13 m) resulted from a low dam across Pena Creek and appeared to be several decades old. Cattails (Typha) bordered the open water, which was almost completely choked with a dense stand of pondweed (Potamogeton), forming a solid mat just below the surface. The jacana spent most of its time walking on the vegetation mat and feeding actively, presumably on aquatic insects. At one point, it captured, dispatched, and consumed a large dragonfly. The bird was wary and alert, flying to the center of the pond and calling loudly if approached too closely or disturbed. It would remain there, watchful for a while, before resuming feeding.

Marathon lies about equidistant—some 800 km—from resident Northern Jacana populations on the west coast in Sinaloa and on the east coast in southern Texas and Tamaulipas. It is less than half again as far from resident populations on the Mexican Plateau, southward in Guanajuato, Jalisco, and Michoacán. There are scattered inland Texas records, presumably from the eastern population, in Real (American Birds 34:177, 1980), Kerr (American Birds 40:492 and 1223, 1986), Uvalde, Bexar, Webb, and Victoria counties (Oberholser, H.C., The Bird Life of Texas, Vol. 1:306, 1974; University of Texas Press, Austin), though not in Mitchell County. An immature jacana was also noted upriver in the Rio Grande valley at Santa Ana National Wildlife Refuge, Hidalgo County, from November 10 to 30, 1982 (American Birds 37:200, 1983).

Of interest is a Pacific storm, Hurricane Paul, which crossed the Sinaloa coast in late September and tracked northeastward through the Trans-Pecos region of Texas on September 30, 1982—one week before I discovered the Brewster County bird. Additionally, many impoundments now stretch northward across the Mexican Plateau, from central Mexico through Durango and Chihuahua to the U.S. border. These impoundments, typically recharged during the summer-fall rainy season, seem to provide a northward pathway for several other waterbirds that are similarly common in the central highlands (S.O. Williams, unpubl. data). Because the Brewster County jacana could have arrived from any of these three geographic areas, I believe it is incorrect to assume automatically that it originated from the east coast population.

The recent (June 7, 1985 – January 3, 1986) appearance of an adult jacana near Nogales, Arizona (American Birds 39:946, 1985; 40:311, 1986), which followed the Brewster County sighting, represents only the second record for the southwestern United States. Its origin remains uncertain, as there is only one record from adjacent Sonora—a specimen labeled only Sonora, 1961 (S.M. Russell, pers. comm.).

With the material before me, I find no difficulty in recognizing the sexes accurately.

264 THE WILSON BULLETIN Vol. III, No. 2, June 1999

The cornaceous flaps covering the nostrils of the Thinocopridae (Thinocorus spp., Attagis gayi) appear to be placed at the base of the bill. It seems that the basal placement of the nostrils is ancestral in the group, and that forward displacement in jacanas is a derived character. While we cannot confirm that breathing while submerged was a significant selective force in the forward displacement of jacana nostrils, their current position should facilitate it.

Young jacanas are known to avoid predators or aggressive conspecifics by taking to the water, and snorkeling behavior is shared with other species. The chicks of the Northern Jacana, which is considered to form a superspecies with the Wattled Jacana, have been reported to swim, hide in the water, and submerge with only their bills and the tops of their heads showing above the surface. The hiding behavior of young Pheasent-tailed Jacanas (Hydrophasianus chirurgus) from India and Asia appears similar; chicks may freeze while hiding under a leaf or even while completely submerged except for the bill. The chicks, and sometimes even the adults, of the Lesser Jacana (Microparra capensis) of Africa are also known to submerge with only their bills out of the water.

Since snorkeling seems to be accompanied by anatomical adaptations, it is likely that these species also have forward-displaced nostrils. In fact, this appears to be the case in the Northern and Pheasent-tailed Jacanas. For the Lesser Jacana, it is difficult to judge from available pictures. Other species of jacana for which we lack information on snorkeling behavior also have nostrils placed forward along the bill, most notably the African Jacana (Actophilornis africanus). A broader survey would be necessary to determine if snorkeling and forward placement of the nostrils are shared by all species of the family.

In similar aquatic habitats in the central Llanos of Venezuela, the young of at least three other species swim or dive, although adults do not. The altricial nestlings of Hoatzins (Opisthocomus hoazin) and Greater Anis (Crotophaga major) jump from their nests and swim or dive in the water below. The precocial chicks of Purple Gallinules (Porphyrula martinica) dive when threatened. Interestingly, the latter and the congeneric P. flavirostris have nostrils displaced forward along the bill.

Similar Breeding Systems in Other Birds

Jenni (1973) reviewed avian social systems in which females commonly lay more than one clutch in rapid succession. In these systems, females either lay clutches that are incubated by more than one male (polyandry), or they lay one clutch attended by a male and a second which they attend themselves. Since there is no specific term for both of these strategies, I will refer to them as rapid multi-clutch systems. 

Research on rapid multi-clutch species has resulted in several hypotheses that may explain the evolution of the Mountain Plover social system. Text: RUDDY TURNSTONE (Arenaria interpres morinelia). Turnstones are unusual in form, in that the bill is quite stout, pointed and has an upturned appearance since the top of the upper mandibleis perfectly straight. The present handsome species breeds on the Arctic coast and migrates abundantly along both coasts, wintering from southern United States southward. The common Turnstone, a grayer variety, is an Old World species, a few of which breed in western Alaska and migrate through Japan. The Turnstone is commonly known among sportsmen as Calico-back, Horse-foot Snipe and Beach Snipe.

The Snail Kite Rostrhamus sociabilis) is a highly specialized raptor that ranges from southern Florida and Mexico, through Central America, to Bolivia, northern Argentina and Uruguay (Beissinger 1988). The kite uses its exceptionally thin upper mandible to extract snails from their shells (Snyder and Snyder 1969). The Mexican Jacana is found and breeds within our borders only in southern Texas.

Polyandry in the Spotted Sandpiper

Polyandry, as it appears in ornithological literature, is one of those anthropomorphic misnomers that necessitate defining whenever it is used. In humans, it literally means that a woman has many husbands at the same time, any one of whom could be the father of her children. In birds, a polyandrous female may have many mates, all of which could contribute genes to each clutch of eggs. 

Until recently, there have been no reports in birds of anything approximating this definition. However, Ridpath (1972) discusses breeding trios consisting of a female and two males in the Tasmanian Native Hen (Tribonyx mortierii). He recorded both males copulating at least once with the female in most trios. Jenni and Collier (1972) described polyandry in a population of the American Jacana (Jacana spinosa) on a seven-acre pond in Costa Rica. They observed that one female copulated with three different males in a twenty-minute period, and another copulated with four different males in a single afternoon. Molnar (1950) reported more than one male cuckoo copulating with a female.

If the copulations reported in these instances function in transferring active sperm to the oviduct of the female with ova ready to be fertilized, then several males could copulate successfully with a single female in a matter of minutes, hours, or even days, and the resulting clutch of eggs could be the combined effort of a kind of copulatory roulette. If, on the other hand, the observed copulations do not function in this way, the act itself could serve to establish a bond between individuals and could or could not help to coordinate their reproductive efforts for a later period.

Many ornithologists have focused in recent years on avian social systems, relating the disciplines of behavior and ecology in their fieldwork. Two such studies appear here. I was excited to learn, when conversing with Helen Hays in November 1971, that in her study of Spotted Sandpipers on Great Gull Island, she had discovered serial polyandry. I was elated when she consented to submit her work to *The Living Bird*, which she did in March 1972. Early in the summer of 1972, while teaching at the University of Minnesota’s Biological Station at Lake Itasca, I learned of Lewis Oring’s work there on the same species and that he, too, had found serial polyandry among his marked birds. He was acquainted with Miss Hays’s study through an abstract she had submitted for a symposium at the upcoming meeting of the American Ornithologists Union. I solicited Lewis Oring’s paper in July. It seemed appropriate for *The Living Bird* to publish two papers on the mating system of the same species by two ornithologists conducting independent studies in regions as far apart as Minnesota and New York.

The tibia is about half as long as the tarsus, transversely scutellate or ocreate (booted) both anteriorly and posteriorly. The middle toe, without a claw, is about as long as the tarsus or slightly shorter. The outer toe is about the same length, and the inner toe is slightly shorter. The claw is slender, compressed, acute, straight or sometimes slightly recurved terminally. The claws of the anterior toes are similar in form to that of the hallux but much shorter, about as long as the basal phalanx of the middle toe. The interdigital spaces are completely cleft.

The Mexican Jacana (Jacana spinosa) is about 8 inches long. It is a very peculiar species with a bill resembling that of a plover, featuring a leaf-like sheaf at the base that covers the forehead. It has a hard spur on the shoulder of each wing, and its legs and toes are extremely long, with the toenails being abnormally large; the hind nail can often be an inch and a half long. In the case of the Mountain Plover, Graul (pers. commun.) showed that the mating system is complex and variable, and he attributes its evolution largely to the lack of stability in their short-grass prairie environment. Considering the extreme conditions under which Sanderlings nest in the high Arctic, there is little doubt that whatever their system eventually proves to be, it will show adaptations for highly unpredictable food supplies, short seasons, and rigorous climatic conditions, in contrast to polyandrous systems which have evolved in areas with high predation rates, long seasons, and abundant food. It appears that various types of polygamous mating systems, including polyandrous ones, are more common among shorebirds than previously supposed. Within the suborder Charadrii, certain species occupy some of the harshest Arctic and arid environments, others the temperate forests and grasslands, and still others various tropical habitats. These species are exposed to the diversity of food supplies, season lengths, and predation pressures typical of their environments. In response to this great array of selective pressures, a large variety of social systems has evolved. Where a system of multiple clutches of various types has developed, we find various compromises that reduce female stress. Studies of species exhibiting these compromise characteristics will undoubtedly reveal new and interesting cases of polyandry.

Characteristics of some shorebirds for which polyandry has been demonstrated or suggested include:

- Females are about 3 percent larger than males.
- Egg or clutch size is reduced.
- Females are dominant in courtship.
- Males do most of the incubating.

Mr. J. W. Gregory provided an account of his research on British Paleogene Bryozoa, recognizing thirty species represented in the National Collection by about 750 specimens. Mr. Sclater described a small collection of birds from Anguilla, West Indies, collected by Mr. W. R. Elliott, one of the collectors employed by the Committee for the exploration of the Lesser Antilles. Prof. G. J. Romanes, F.R.S., presented a paper on a seemingly new diagnostic character of primates: the terminal joints of both hands and feet in all species of this order are devoid of hairs, except in lemurs. 

Mr. O. Thomas discussed the genus Zchinops of the order Insectivora and provided notes on the dentition of related genera Zriculus and Centetes. Mr. G. A. Boulenger reported on the reptiles and amphibians collected by Mr. C. Hose on Mount Dulit, North Borneo. Among these was a new lizard of the genus Varanus, proposed to be called V. heteropholis. Two new amphibians were also described: Rhacophorus dulitensis and Nectophryne hosit. 

Lieut. Colonel H. H. Godwin-Austen, F.R.S., read a paper on new species and varieties of the land-mollusk genus Diflommatina, collected by himself and more recently by Mr. W. Doherty in the Naga and Munipur Hill ranges. The author described twenty-seven presumed new species, notably D. unicrenata, characterized by a peculiarly formed peristome. 

A communication from Mr. B. B. Woodward discussed the mode of growth and structure of the shell in Velates conotdeus, Lamk., and other Neritidae. The growth process involves an initial normal phase, followed by a change in growth direction, with the shell enlarging by adding new shelly material on the exterior of the underside and removing previously formed layers on the inner surface. The internal septum, serving as a myophore, originated in the paries, which was replaced by the septum during growth. Velates conotdeus exemplifies life-history conditions found in recent species of the closely related genus Neritina. The paper also described the relationship between the paries and septum in this genus. 

This meeting concludes the current session. The next session (1892–93) will begin in November 1892.
